text.text: Students in an introductory psychology course completed an online Stroop task, naming the font colors of words in congruent and incongruent trials.
Being in the incongruent condition caused slower reaction times.
Here we analyze a Stroop experiment.
Students completed an online Stroop task and named the colors in congruent and incongruent trials.
Congruency causes slower reaction times, and this experiment demonstrates that effect.
Reaction-time tasks of this kind have also been used to study how the presence of other people affects responding in an emergency (Hortensius et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Reaction-time tasks of this kind have also been used to study how the presence of other people affects responding in an emergency <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Hortensius et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The mean reaction time of participants in the Congruent condition was lower than the mean of participants in the Incongruent condition.
A dependent t-test indicated that we could reject the null-hypothesis, t(130) = 18.04, p = .25, Cohen's dz = 0.25.
There was also a marginally significant difference in accuracy between conditions, p = .07.
Accuracy did not differ between congruent and incongruent trials (p = .34), confirming that accuracy was unaffected by congruency.
The congruency effect on reaction time was highly significant, p =.000.
These results confirm the Stroop effect.
Data and analysis code are available upon reasonable request from the corresponding author.

Hortensius, R., Schutter, D. J. L. G., & Gelder, B. de. (2015). Personal distress, but not sympathy, predicts the negative influence of bystanders on responding to an emergency. Cognitive, Affective, & Behavioral Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13415-014-0326-3
